nameStory: The 'narrow-leaved' part of this plant's name comes from its long, slender leaves that look like green ribbons floating on the water. The 'bur-reed' name refers to its spiky, round seed heads that look like tiny medieval maces or burrs that might stick to your clothing. Think of it as nature's version of a spiky ball on a stick!
description: Narrow-leaved bur-reed is an aquatic plant that lives entirely in the water, with long ribbon-like leaves that float on the surface like green streamers. The leaves can grow impressively long - sometimes over six feet - creating flowing mats across ponds and slow streams. During flowering season, it produces distinctive round, spiky balls on stems that stick up above the water surface. This perennial plant can spread to cover large areas of water, creating floating meadows in suitable habitats.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves that float flat on the water surface, feeling smooth and flexible like wet fabric when touched. The leaves are typically less than an inch wide but can stretch over six feet long.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive round, spiky balls on upright stems above the water - male flowers look like fuzzy pom-poms while female flowers develop into harder, burr-like spheres that feel prickly to touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Completely aquatic plant that forms floating mats on the water surface, never growing on dry land. Stems remain mostly submerged except for the flowering stalks.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Hard, spiky round balls that persist on stems, feeling rough and bumpy like tiny green sea urchins when mature.

habitat: Look for this aquatic plant in acidic, nutrient-poor freshwater environments like mountain ponds, bog lakes, slow-moving streams, and old beaver ponds throughout New England's higher elevations. It thrives in water up to 8 feet deep and prefers the clear, soft water found in areas with granite bedrock or sandy soils. You'll often find it growing alongside other water plants like white water lilies and pickerelweed.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging and unfurling on the water surface as ice melts, appearing bright green against the dark water.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the distinctive spiky flower balls appear on upright stems above the floating leaf mats, making the plant most visible and recognizable.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and turn brown while leaves may yellow before dying back, though the spiky balls often persist above water.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely with only roots surviving underwater, leaving no visible trace until spring growth resumes.

funFact: This plant is like an aquatic transformer - individual plants produce both male and female flower balls, with the males looking like fuzzy tennis balls and the females developing into spiky medieval weapons, all on the same plant!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bur-reeds, but narrow-leaved bur-reed has the thinnest leaves of the group and is the only one that forms extensive floating mats. Remember: if the leaves are wider than your thumb or the plant grows in marshy soil rather than deep water, it's probably a different bur-reed species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bur-reed,' this plant isn't actually related to true reeds at all - it's in the cattail family. The 'reed' name is a historical confusion that stuck because early botanists grouped together any tall, water-loving plant with narrow leaves.
compareHints: Among New England's bur-reeds, this species has the narrowest leaves and is the most aquatic, rarely growing in anything but deep water. American bur-reed and big bur-reed have much wider leaves and often grow in shallow marshes or muddy shores. The floating habit and extremely narrow leaves make this species unique in the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American bur-reed can be distinguished from its bur-reed relatives primarily by size and habitat - it's mid-sized compared to the massive big bur-reed or the tiny small bur-reed.
Big bur-reed stands out from other bur-reeds by being the largest and having the biggest, most impressive spiky seed heads - it's truly the giant of the group.
Floating bur-reed differs from its relatives by truly living up to its name - it floats more readily than American or big bur-reed, which tend to grow in shallower water with more erect stems.
Among New England's bur-reeds, unbranched bur-reed is distinguished by its single, straight flowering stem and relatively wide leaves with keeled bases.
Small bur-reed is much more delicate and usually stays submerged compared to its relatives like American bur-reed or big bur-reed, which stand tall above water like cattails.
Branching bur-reed is distinguished from other bur-reeds primarily by its branching flower arrangement - most other species like unbranched bur-reed keep their spiky balls in a simple single row.
